beats.text: A cluster of n servers keeps copies of the same data. It decides a change only when more than half of all n servers accept it. 5 needs 3 so 2 can fail; 4 also needs 3 so only 1 can fail.
Defines accept, decide, quorum size, quorum, and stop, using x = 1 accepted by A, B, C.
leap: "the next change" assumes the changes come in a fixed order, one slot at a time, which is never said. Beat 4's rule ("Each server accepts only one change as the next change") depends on this.

beats.text: A gets no reply from D in 500 ms: crash or partition, A can't tell. With quorum size 2, {A,B} decide x = 1 and {C,D} decide x = 2: split brain.
unsaid: The Shown column switches to 4 servers, after beat 2's 5 servers A–E. The Said column never says the cluster is now 4 servers. The reader has to work this out from the names A–D.
The question this beat answers, "why can't the other 2 go on?", is never asked in the words. The text jumps straight into "A sends to D".
leap: "So suppose quorum size were 2": the words never say that 2 is exactly what 'let the 2 survivors go on' means in a 4-server cluster, or that it is half of 4.

beats.text: Quorum size = majority size floor(n/2)+1. Two groups of 3 among 5 total 6 > 5 places, so they share C. C has already accepted x = 1, so it refuses x = 2. Count all configured servers, not the reachable ones.
unresolved: "6 > 5 places": 'places' is an odd word for this counting step. It is only shown for n = 5, and the general version ('two majorities together have more than n members') is never said.
unsaid: The Shown column has the overlapping groups {A,B,C} and {C,D,E}. The words do not say how C could be in contact with both groups, given that beat 3 framed the problem as a partition.
leap: "Each server accepts only one change as the next change" is a new rule, and the whole argument depends on it. It appears here for the first time, with no reason given.
excess: "D and E reach only each other, and 'more than half of 2' would let them decide" gives away the scenario that beat 5 asks the reader to predict.

beats.text: Predict: {A,B,C} | {D,E}. A, B, C have 3 ≥ 3 and keep deciding. D, E have 2 < 3 and stop.
excess: The prediction was already answered at the end of beat 4 ("D and E reach only each other..."), so the test gives the reader nothing new to work out.

beats.text: Tolerance = n − majority size. A table for n = 3..7 shows that 4 and 5 both need 3. Adding a server to an odd-sized cluster raises the majority size, so tolerance stays the same and each change waits for one more accept.
unsaid: The table rows for n = 3, 6 and 7 are shown but not read aloud. Minor.

beats.text: 5 survives 2 and 4 survives 1 because both need 3, and 3 is the smallest group that must share a server with any other. Use odd sizes. Assumes servers crash but never lie; see the Raft and PBFT papers.

blocking: Beat 4: "Each server accepts only one change as the next change". This rule makes the shared server C refuse x = 2, and it is introduced here without warning or reason. Without it, overlapping groups prove nothing.
Beat 3: the switch from 5 servers to 4 is not said in words (it appears only in Shown), so the reader rereads to find out which cluster they are in.
cuts: Beat 4: cut the D/E sentence ("Count all n configured servers... would let them decide"), or move it into beat 5's answer. It currently spoils the prediction.
Beat 7: cut "leader election, and reads are covered in the Raft and PBFT papers". It brings in unknown names right at the close; "servers crash but never lie" is enough as the scope.

question.text: Why can a 5-server cluster lose 2 servers while a 4-server cluster can lose only 1? Known from Beat 1, where it is the title.
question.result_stated: Yes, Beat 1: "For 5 servers that is 3, so 5 − 3 = 2 servers can fail. For 4 servers it is also 3, so only 4 − 3 = 1 can fail."

reply.motive: There is a reason for the approach in Beat 1, "The rest explains why the rule is 'more than half'", and in Beat 3's objection, "A sees the same silence in both cases". A reason to care about the question is missing from the words. The plan's point that "the 4th server costs money but buys nothing" is never said; only Beat 6's "tolerance stays the same" and Beat 7's "Use odd cluster sizes" hint at it.
reply.close: Yes, Beat 7: "5 survives 2 and 4 survives 1 because both need 3 servers, and 3 is the smallest group that must share a server with any other group." The general argument (overlap means a shared server, and that server refuses a conflicting change) is said in words, though the refusal rule itself comes late, in Beat 4.
reply.recap: A cluster only decides a change when more than half of all its servers agree, so two groups can never both decide different things; that means 4 servers need 3 just like 5 do, so the 4th server buys you no extra failure tolerance.
reply.strongest: Beat 3: "A sees the same silence in both cases" makes it concrete why the survivors cannot simply carry on, and leads straight into split brain.
reply.weakest: Beat 4: it packs the formula, the overlap count ("6 > 5 places"), a brand-new one-vote-per-slot rule, and the counting caveat that gives away Beat 5 into one beat.
suggestions: Introduce the rule "a server accepts only one change for each slot" in Beat 2, alongside accept.
Say the general overlap argument in words: two groups that are each more than half of n together have more than n members, so they must share a server.
Say in Beat 3's words that the cluster is now 4 servers and that a quorum of 2 is exactly half.
Add the cost motive to Beat 1: a 4th server costs money but buys no extra tolerance.
